edits.replace:
Asked outside `#boundary` at all four direct writes, and that ordering is what keeps a write from refusing itself: the rung is asked before the depth is raised, and the tail of the write asks no rung at all. A refused call is not inside a callback and has nothing to survive, which is the same reason `#writeValues` puts its refusal outside the boundary. See ADR-069 and ADR-070.

It also out-ranks the resolution of whatever the verb was handed, and that order has one owner rather than one per member. Tier 0 always had it: `#setTrigger` and `#setStagger` ask this rung and resolve inside `#boundary` afterwards, which is ADR-061's order and `RA-36` pins it there. Tier 2 did not, because `#writeValues` took a resolved entry and an argument expression is evaluated before the member that would refuse it, so the order was a property of how four call sites happened to nest two expressions rather than something anything owned. The entry arrives as a thunk now, and `#setKeyframe` and `#removeKeyframe` ask this rung one line above their own resolve, which is the same call moved rather than a second one. What that buys is a true diagnosis instead of a false one: a write aimed at the node an in-flight commit is compiling answers `schema-commit-reentrant` rather than `Unknown graph node`, which is false, because that node exists and is compiled in a map the caller cannot see. See ADR-070's amendment.

Asked twice on one path, and that is the cheaper guarantee rather than sloppiness. `#setKeyframe` asks it and may then reach `#writeValues`, which asks it again. Both asks are a pair of field reads with no side effect on either branch, and nothing between them can change either field, so the second cannot answer differently. A variant of `#writeValues` that skipped the rung for an internal caller would be one member with two contracts, and the first caller to pick the wrong one would get no refusal at all. Neither call is dead, stated here so a later reader does not delete one, and `#recompileKeyframes` asks no rung for the same reason read the other way round: both of its callers just did, and it is a tail rather than an entry point.

The assignment is unconditional, and it is safe to be unconditional only because nothing can have written the retained pair since `#derive` read it. Every in-place write is refused while the depth is up, so the four members that reach `#tracks.set` and `#motions.set` outside a commit are unreachable from inside one. Without that refusal this assignment silently deletes an `overlay` and a `liveWrite` the composition is still honouring, along with the retained definition a `setValues` rewrote beside them, which is the defect issue #309 owns. Merging the two pairs instead was refused rather than unconsidered: a merge preserves those fields while the definition they describe is the commit's, so `liveWrite` would claim a write against a Track built from a definition that never took it, which is the opposite of the conservative direction ADR-066 chose for that field. See ADR-070's amendment and ADR-066.

The entry arrives as a thunk rather than as a value, and the two are not interchangeable. An argument expression is evaluated before this member is entered, so a resolved entry means the retained pair was read before the rung was asked, and inside a commit that read is wrong twice over: it resolves against a pair the commit is about to replace, and for a node the commit is adding it answers `Unknown graph node`, which is false. The thunk is what makes the order this member's own rather than a property of how its four call sites nest two expressions, and the two resolutions stay different on purpose: a handle resolves by id and token through `#writableEntry` and refuses a stale handle, a public verb resolves by id through `#entryOf` and refuses an unknown one. Neither rung moves, and the rule that the `#writable` rungs are not in the handle factory is untouched, because the factory still names `#writableEntry` and only names it lazily. `## #refuseReentrant` owns the order. See ADR-070's amendment.

## Amendment, 2026-09-05: the rung out-ranks the resolution, so a refused write reads the condition rather than a false absence

The Consequences above name what issue #309 had left once this rung shipped: its four in-place write paths land here, so what remains distinctly its own is the order between the refusal and the entry resolution. This is that order, decided here rather than in a record of its own, because splitting one rule across two documents would make the next reader ask which of them governs `#setKeyframe`. Nothing about the condition, the name, the `ruleId` or the message changes. [Issue #309](https://github.com/chahyasantoso/motion5/issues/309).

**The two tiers had opposite orders, and one of them was already right.** `#setTrigger` and `#setStagger` ask this rung and then resolve, which is ADR-061's order and `RA-36` pins it. `#writeValues` took a resolved `TrackEntry`, and an argument expression is evaluated before the member that would refuse it, so the rung inside it was asked second at all four of its call sites and the order was a property of how each of them happened to nest two expressions rather than something anything owned. `#setKeyframe` and `#removeKeyframe` are the same shape one line apart.

**What that cost is a false diagnosis rather than a lost write, and saying so is half of this amendment.** This record's rung already refuses every one of those four paths, so from inside a commit no seam is reached and no retained entry moves: issue #309's three consequences -- a retained definition the composition has moved past, a cleared overlay over a still-patched timeline, and a deleted `liveWrite` -- are unreachable rather than repaired, which is the strongest form the answer can take, because there is no partial state left for a later slice to reconcile and no compensation path to keep correct. What a caller read was still wrong. A write aimed at the node an in-flight commit is compiling resolved against the retained pair, which does not carry it, and answered `Unknown graph node "x"`. That is false: the node exists, compiled by an effect that already ran, in a map the caller cannot see. A write through a handle whose token has been retired answered a staleness, which is true of the handle and is not the reason the call may not run. A false absence sends a caller looking for a bug in the id it passed; an unordered pair of true answers sends it nowhere. So the refusal precedes the resolution.

**The decision: a refusal meant to out-rank a resolution takes that resolution as a thunk.** `#writeValues` takes `() => TrackEntry` and calls it inside its boundary, after the rung. The two resolutions stay different, which is the whole point of a thunk rather than a shared resolver: a handle resolves by id and token through `#writableEntry` and refuses a stale handle, a public verb resolves by id through `#entryOf` and refuses an unknown one. Neither rung moves, and `project-runtime.md`'s rule that the `#writable` rungs are not in the handle factory is untouched, because the factory still names `#writableEntry` and only names it lazily.

**`#setKeyframe` and `#removeKeyframe` cannot take one, so the refusal moves instead.** Both need `entry.track.keyframes` through `#boundGroup` before either of their two paths is describable at all, so a thunk there would defer a read they immediately have to perform. The rung moves above the resolve, which is the same call one line up rather than a second call, and no condition is copied anywhere.

**The rung is asked twice on the `#setKeyframe` path, and that is the cheaper guarantee.** It is a pair of field reads with no side effect on either branch, and nothing between the two asks can change either field, so the second cannot answer differently. The alternative is a variant of `#writeValues` that skips the rung for an internal caller, which is one member with two contracts and no refusal at all for the first caller to pick the wrong one. Neither call is dead, and `project-runtime.md` says so under `## #refuseReentrant` so a later reader does not delete one. `#recompileKeyframes` asks no rung and does not start, because both of its callers just did and it is a tail rather than an entry point.

**The invariant this buys `#adoptMaps`, written down where the assignment is.** That member replaces the retained pair unconditionally, and it is safe to be unconditional only because nothing can have written that pair since `#derive` read it. Every in-place write is refused while the depth is up, so the four members that reach `#tracks.set` and `#motions.set` outside a commit are unreachable from inside one. That claim lived nowhere before this amendment, and `project-runtime.md`'s `## #adoptMaps` is where it lives now, which is the one place everybody who edits the commit path reads.

**Making `#adoptMaps` merge rather than assign was the most tempting alternative, and it is wrong in a way worth recording.** A merge would preserve `overlay` and `liveWrite` from the retained pair while the definition they describe is the commit's, so `liveWrite: true` would claim a write against a Track built from a definition that never took it. That is over-reporting, which is the opposite of the conservative direction ADR-066 chose for that field, and it cannot preserve the rewrite a `setValues` made to the retained definition either, which is the consequence ADR-060 cares about most. It also makes the answer to what `handle.definition` says depend on whether a commit is on the stack.

**Consequences.** No public surface moves. The one signature change is on a `#private` member, and no export, type, schema, message or `ruleId` changes. Three paths that answered a false `ruleId` from inside a commit now answer `schema-commit-reentrant`: a live write aimed at a node the commit is adding, and both live-write entry points reached through a retired handle. [GUARDRAILS.md](./GUARDRAILS.md) carries the general rule, and [LIVE-EDIT-COST.md](./LIVE-EDIT-COST.md)'s seam bullet carries the caller-facing half.

**Evidence.** `RA-136` through `RA-139` in `structural-commit-path.test.ts`. `RA-138` is the only red one, and that is reported rather than engineered: this record's own rung already refuses all four paths, so `RA-136` and `RA-137` are green on both sides and the file says so, per the guardrail against padding a red count by asserting less in the cases that could not fail. What they add is the first measurement of the refusal on the write path issue #309 owns rather than on the publishing verbs this record was about, and what they assert is that the seam is never called, which answers for all three of that issue's consequences at once. `RA-139` is the accepting direction, and it shows both thunks resolving rather than merely deferring.

**What this leaves open.** Issue #313, a seam on those same four paths that fails rather than disposing or being adopted over. Neither the boundary nor this rung can see it: `#writeValues`' escalation and `#recompileKeyframes`' `staged.commit()` both run after the retained entry has moved, on paths that never reach `#apply`. That slice reorders the tails this one changes the signature of, so it lands after it.

- A refusal meant to out-rank a resolution takes that resolution as a thunk, because an argument expression is evaluated before the member that would refuse it. `ProjectRuntime` had two tiers asking one rung in opposite orders and only one of them was right: the tier 0 verbs asked and then resolved, while `#writeValues` took a resolved entry, so the rung inside it was asked second at every one of its four call sites and the order was a property of how each site happened to nest two expressions rather than something anything owned, with `#setKeyframe` and `#removeKeyframe` the same shape one line apart. What it cost was not a lost write, because the rung already refused all four paths -- it was a false diagnosis. A write aimed at the node an in-flight commit was compiling resolved against a retained pair that does not carry it and answered `Unknown graph node "x"`, which is false, because that node exists and is compiled in a map the caller cannot see, and one made through a retired handle answered a staleness that is true of the handle and is not why the call may not run. Three parts generalise. A false absence is strictly worse than an unordered pair of true answers, because it sends a caller looking for a bug in the id it passed rather than at the call it made, so where two answers to one call are both available the one the condition owns goes first. A member that cannot take a thunk, because it needs the resolved thing to describe its own work at all, moves its refusal up a line instead, which is the same call rather than a second one, so the order costs no copy of a condition either way. And a rung asked twice on one path is cheaper than a variant of the shared member that skips it: two side-effect-free field reads cannot answer differently, while one member with two contracts gives no refusal at all to the first caller that picks the wrong one, so both calls are documented as load-bearing rather than one of them deleted as dead. The bullet above is this same shape one question earlier: that one is about which of two conditions a rung asks first, and this one is about whether the rung is asked before the lookup it out-ranks. [Issue #309](https://github.com/chahyasantoso/motion5/issues/309).

All four now run at the same in-flight depth a commit uses: the write completes its phase, skips its flush, and reports `ProjectRuntime is disposed.` once, with the release drained at the boundary afterwards. `#committing` becomes `#inFlight` because five members read it, the raise and the drain move into one `#boundary` member rather than four copies of `#apply`'s `finally`, and `#writeValues` loses its inline flush to `#invalidateOne`, which owns the skip and the report in one statement. - **An in-place write from a hook is discarded by the commit that called it.** [Issue #309](https://github.com/chahyasantoso/motion5/issues/309). The third and last mechanism on the same four members, after the disposal #305 answered and the adoption #309 answered, and the one neither the boundary nor the rung can see: `#writeValues`' escalation and `#recompileKeyframes`' `staged.commit()` both run after the retained entry has moved, on paths that never reach `#apply`. Two of the four ask a seam after the point of no return and two ask it before, for one condition, so a `stageTrack` or a `commit()` that throws leaves the retained entry claiming a rebase, an overlay and a `liveWrite` the composition never took, and a staged Track nothing holds.
